issues.legal_issue: A High Court may reappraise evidence in a second appeal when the first appellate court’s decision results from a procedural error affecting its treatment of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court rejected the claim, treating revenue records and rent receipts as suspect or insufficient.
The High Court considered that the lower appellate court had ignored material documentary evidence and reassessed the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reappraise the evidence and reach its own conclusion because the lower appellate court had ignored the weight of relevant documents.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an error in appreciating evidence on the merits alone is not a procedural defect, even if it produces a seriously erroneous finding. A procedural defect may arise where the lower appellate court places the burden on the wrong party, rejects admissible evidence, or ignores the weight of evidence and is influenced by inconsequential matters. The Court relied on Madan Lal v. Gopi, AIR 1980 SC 1754, and referred to V. Ramachandra Ayyar v. Ramalingam Chettiar, AIR 1963 SC 302.

rule.if: second_appeal and (wrong_burden_of_proof or admissible_evidence_rejected or material_evidence_ignored)

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a lower appellate court’s decision.
predicates.wrong_burden_of_proof: The lower appellate court placed the burden of proof on the wrong party and that approach substantially affected its finding.
predicates.admissible_evidence_rejected: The lower appellate court rejected evidence that was admissible.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The lower appellate court ignored the weight of material evidence or allowed inconsequential matters to influence its judgment.

issues.definition: When a second appeal involves a specified procedural error in the lower appellate court’s treatment of evidence, the High Court may reappraise that evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A genuine entry recording a subtenant in the prescribed land record supports that person’s adhivasi status, and an heir in continued possession may rely on the entry where its genuineness has not been rebutted.
material_facts: The prescribed khasra entry recorded the claimant’s father as a subtenant.
The opposing parties did not prove that the entry had been introduced surreptitiously out of ill-will or hostility.
Later khasra entries named the claimant as a person in possession, and rent receipts were evidence of subtenancy and possession.
The lower courts had rejected the claim in part because they considered the entry suspicious and found no contract or subtenancy proved.
issues.conclusion: The entry’s genuineness had to be presumed in the absence of evidence that it was surreptitiously introduced; the entry, later possession records, and rent receipts supported the claimant’s subtenancy-based adhivasi claim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, makes the prescribed Khasra or Khatauni entry the basis for adhivasi status and eliminates a separate enquiry into possession for accepting that record. Under Sections 28 and 33 of the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, the relevant record was prepared; an entry recording a subtenant identifies that person as occupant. The Court relied on Amba Prasad v. Abdul Noor Khan, [1964] 7 SCR 800, and Nath Singh v. Board of Revenue, [1968] 3 SCR 498. An opposing party must show that the entry was introduced surreptitiously out of ill-will or hostility to displace the presumption of genuineness.

rule.if: adhivasi_claim_based_on_revenue_entry and prescribed_record_names_claimant_or_predecessor_as_subtenant and not surreptitious_entry_proved and successor_continued_in_possession

predicates.adhivasi_claim_based_on_revenue_entry: The proceeding involves a claim to adhivasi status based on an entry in a prescribed land record.
predicates.prescribed_record_names_claimant_or_pred: The prescribed land record names the claimant or the claimant’s predecessor as a subtenant.
predicates.surreptitious_entry_proved: The opposing party proved that the entry was introduced surreptitiously out of ill-will or hostility.
predicates.successor_continued_in_possession: The claimant, as successor to the recorded subtenant, was shown in later records or other evidence to have continued in possession.

issues.definition: A claimant to adhivasi status may rely on a prescribed entry recording the claimant or a predecessor as subtenant when the entry’s surreptitious introduction is not proved and a successor continued in possession.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate for failure to substitute deceased parties who are only formal parties when the controversy can be decided among the remaining parties.
material_facts: Certain defendants died while the appeal was pending, and no substitution application was filed for them.
Those defendants were proforma parties, and the High Court held that the appeal could proceed without their substitution.
issues.conclusion: The appeal did not abate because the deceased defendants were only proforma parties.
issues.legal_principle: Whether an appeal is properly constituted after a party’s death depends on whether the necessary parties for deciding the controversy remain before the court. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, [1962] 2 SCR 636.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal in which a party died before the appeal was decided.
predicates.deceased_parties_are_formal_parties: The deceased parties were only formal parties to the controversy.
predicates.controversy_can_be_decided_without_them: The dispute can be decided between the appellant and the remaining respondents without the deceased parties.

issues.definition: An appeal continues when deceased parties were only formal parties and the remaining parties are sufficient to decide the controversy.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court may hear a suit for injunction when title arises only incidentally, even if revenue courts have exclusive jurisdiction over matters otherwise assigned to them.
material_facts: The suit sought a permanent injunction against interference with possession.
The question of title arose only incidentally in deciding the injunction suit.
The defendants objected that revenue courts had exclusive jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to try the injunction suit because title arose only incidentally.
issues.legal_principle: The exclusive jurisdiction of revenue courts does not bar a civil suit for injunction when the question of title arises only incidentally.

predicates.civil_suit_for_injunction: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking an injunction.
predicates.title_arises_only_incidentally: The court needs to consider title only as an incidental matter in deciding the injunction suit.

issues.definition: A civil court may hear an injunction suit when title is only incidental to the dispute.
